title: Out to Samaria and down the desert road
sum: Stephen's death sets off a persecution, and Saul leads it, raiding homes in Jerusalem. The scattered believers carry the message with them. Philip, one of the Seven, goes to Samaria, a people Jews had quarreled with for centuries, and the city welcomes the Messiah he announces, with healings and exorcisms and great joy. Even Simon, a magician the Samaritans had hailed as the Power of God, believes and is baptized. But the Spirit has not yet come on the Samaritans until Peter and John arrive from Jerusalem and lay hands on them. When Simon tries to buy that power, Peter curses his money and calls him to repent.

Then an angel sends Philip onto the empty road to Gaza, where he meets a eunuch, the finance minister of the queen of Kush, riding home from worship in Jerusalem and reading Isaiah 53 aloud. Philip starts from that passage and tells him the good news about Jesus, and at the first water the man asks what stops him from being baptized. Nothing does. The Spirit snatches Philip away, and the eunuch goes home rejoicing. In one chapter the word has crossed two of Israel's oldest boundaries: to the Samaritans, and to a foreigner the Law kept out of the assembly.
readings: The chapter fits what is known of the region: Samaria's old capital rebuilt by Herod as Sebaste, the coastal towns of Azotus and Caesarea, the kingdom of Kush with its ruling queens titled Kandake, and the magicians who worked the cities of the Roman East. Historians debate how much of the detail comes from Philip himself, whom Luke says he met at Caesarea (21:8, a "we" passage), and how much is Luke's shaping. Simon Magus is the only person in the chapter who reappears in other early sources, and there he has grown into a legend.

Jesus said the apostles would be his witnesses "in Jerusalem, and in all of Judea and Samaria, and as far as the farthest end of the earth" (1:8). Chapter 8 moves the story from the first stage to the second and gives a first sign of the third: a man from Ethiopia, which Greeks thought of as the edge of the world. Each step is driven by God, through persecution, an angel and the Spirit, more than by any plan of the church.
Read as a story of outsiders

Samaritans, a magician and a eunuch: everyone Philip meets stands at or beyond the edge of Israel's community. Luke shows the gospel reaching the people Israel's own prophets had promised to gather (Isaiah 56:3–8), before it reaches the full Gentiles of chapter 10.

views.H: Philip's "city of Samaria" is probably Sebaste, a largely pagan city, or a Samaritan town nearby such as Sychar or Gitta. The kingdom of Kush (Meroë, in modern Sudan) traded with Egypt and Rome, and its queens, called kandake, are known from Greek and Roman writers and from their pyramids. The road to Gaza ran southwest from Jerusalem toward the coast and Egypt.
views.C: Many critical scholars see two traditions joined here: Philip's mission (8:5–13, 26–40) and a Jerusalem story of Peter and Simon (8:14–25), which Luke has combined to show Jerusalem approving new work. The delay of the Spirit in 8:16 is often explained as a result of that joining (Haenchen). Others defend the unity of the account. The added verse 8:37 is a clear case of the church's practice entering the text.
views.L: Luke builds the eunuch's story like the Emmaus story at the end of his Gospel (Luke 24:13–35): a road, a stranger, Scripture opened about a suffering Messiah, a sacrament, and a sudden disappearance. Within Acts, Philip's journey from Jerusalem to Samaria to the coast to Caesarea traces the widening circles of 1:8.
views.J: Samaritans and Jews shared the books of Moses but had split over the true place of worship, Gerizim or Jerusalem. That the first mission outside Jerusalem goes to Samaria shows the movement still thinking of the restoration of all Israel, north and south. The eunuch, a worshiper of Israel's God barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1, is the Isaiah 56 hope come true.
views.T: Catholic and Orthodox teaching finds in 8:14–17 the roots of confirmation and chrismation, and the word "simony" comes from 8:18–24. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church honors the eunuch as the first to bring the faith to its land, Ethiopia. The fathers loved the eunuch's humility in asking for a guide (Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts).

deep.h: Where does the Spirit come in?
deep.b:
Acts has no single pattern for how believers receive the Spirit. At Pentecost Peter promises the Spirit to all who repent and are baptized (2:38). In Samaria baptized believers wait until apostles lay hands on them (8:14–17). At Caesarea the Spirit falls before baptism, with no hands laid on anyone (10:44–48). At Ephesus it comes right after baptism, when Paul lays on hands (19:5–6). The eunuch is baptized and goes on his way rejoicing, with no mention of the Spirit at all, except in a few manuscripts that add it (see the variant at 8:39).

Readers have drawn very different conclusions. Some see Luke describing new situations as God met them, with each "first" (Samaritans, Gentiles, John's disciples) marked by a visible sign. Some build a normal pattern from 2:38 and treat the others as exceptions (James Dunn). Pentecostals see a pattern of a second experience after conversion (Roger Stronstad). Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches see the laying on of hands as the root of a rite that completes baptism. The card on this chapter sets these side by side.

Luke gives three facts: he was from "Ethiopia," the kingdom of Kush on the upper Nile; he was a eunuch; and he was a high official of its queen. He had made a long pilgrimage to Jerusalem, owned a scroll of Isaiah in Greek, and was reading it. Luke never says whether he was a Jew, a convert or a Gentile God-fearer, perhaps on purpose. His presence answers Psalm 68:31 and Zephaniah 3:10, and his question, "What is stopping me?", answers Deuteronomy 23:1 with Isaiah 56:3–5.

In modern times African and African American Christians have taken him as a sign that Africa belonged to the church from the first days, before Europe; scholars such as Clarice Martin have asked why his African identity was so often overlooked in Western commentary. Ethiopian Christians count him as the first evangelist of their land, though the faith reached the kingdom of Aksum through Frumentius in the 300s.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Isaiah 53 opens onto Isaiah 56
deep.b: The eunuch is reading Isaiah 53, and Philip begins from there (8:35). Three chapters later, Isaiah promises the foreigner and the eunuch that they will not be cut off, and that God's house will be called "a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7). I suggest Luke expected readers who knew Isaiah to finish the scroll in their heads: the servant who "was cut off" (Isaiah 53:8) wins a place for the eunuch who feared being "a dried-up tree" (Isaiah 56:3), one with no descendants, just as the servant's own "generation" is in question (8:33). If so, the eunuch's question in 8:36 is the climax of a reading that runs from Isaiah 53 to Isaiah 56. The link between this story and Isaiah 56 is noted by many scholars (for example F. Scott Spencer); the suggestion that Luke means the "generation" line to speak to a childless reader is my own emphasis.

echoes: Deuteronomy 18:15; Deuteronomy 23:1; Deuteronomy 29:18; 1 Kings 18:12; 2 Kings 2:16; Psalm 68:31; Isaiah 53:7–8; Isaiah 56:3–7; Isaiah 58:6; Zephaniah 3:10; Luke 9:52–55; Luke 24:13–35; John 4:4–42; 1:8; 6:5; 11:19; 19:1–7; 21:8–9

settings.what: Philip's preaching in Samaria
settings.to: the crowds of "the city of Samaria," Samaritans who worshiped Israel's God at Mount Gerizim
settings.when: after the persecution that followed Stephen's death drove him out of Jerusalem
settings.why: Philip announces the Messiah to a people who looked for a prophet like Moses, and his healings and exorcisms show that the age of restoration has come to them too. Knowing the hearers were Samaritans changes the message: the promise to Israel is offered to the northern half that Jerusalem had written off.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the scene showed that the church's mission beyond Jerusalem began among people already half inside Israel, and that persecution had spread the word rather than stopped it.

settings.what: Simon's offer, Peter's rebuke and Simon's reply
settings.to: Peter and John, and then Simon, the baptized magician, with the Samaritan believers present
settings.when: after Simon sees the Spirit given through the apostles' hands
settings.why: Simon asks to buy the power to give the Spirit (8:19), treating it like the magic he once practiced for gain. Peter's curse and call to repent show that the Spirit is God's gift, not a power to be traded. His words echo the Law and the prophets (Deuteronomy 29:18; Isaiah 58:6) and leave the door open: "Perhaps he will forgive you." Simon's reply (8:24) asks the apostles to pray for him but does not say he repents, and Luke leaves him there. For a new church in a city impressed by magic, the scene drew a sharp line between the gospel and the wonder-working trade.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, who lived among magicians, healers and paid religious experts, the scene warned that faith and gifts cannot be bought, and later readers took it as a warning against buying church office.

settings.what: The angel's and the Spirit's orders to Philip
settings.by: an angel of the Lord, then the Spirit
settings.to: Philip, in Samaria and then on the road
settings.when: after the Samaritan mission
settings.why: The orders give no reasons: go south to an empty road, then stick close to one chariot. Philip's quick obedience is the point. The mission to the ends of the earth is directed by God step by step, not planned by the church.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the story assured them that the spread of the gospel to Africa and the Gentile world was God's own doing.

settings.what: Philip and the eunuch on Isaiah 53, and the request for baptism
settings.to: the eunuch, a high official of the queen of Kush, reading Isaiah in Greek in his chariot
settings.when: on the road from Jerusalem toward Gaza, as the eunuch returns home from worship
settings.why: The eunuch admits he needs a guide (8:31) and asks whom Isaiah means (8:34): the prophet himself, or someone else. Philip starts from that passage to tell him about Jesus, the servant who suffered in silence and was cut off. For a man who had been to Jerusalem but was kept from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1), the good news meant full belonging, and his own request follows: "What is stopping me from being baptized?" (8:36).
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the scene modeled how the church read its Bible: Isaiah's servant is Jesus, and the Scriptures open to anyone, even the farthest outsider, through someone who explains them.
views: Some think Luke saw the eunuch as a Jew or convert from the far south, so that Cornelius (chapter 10) remains the first true Gentile.
Many think he was a Gentile who worshiped Israel's God, since a eunuch could not become a full convert; Luke leaves it vague so that the story points ahead to the Gentile mission.

traditions.q: Philip baptized the Samaritans, but the Spirit came only when Peter and John came from Jerusalem and laid hands on them (8:14–17). Does giving the Spirit belong to a rite reserved for the apostles and their successors?
views: Yes, in a sense: from this time the apostles gave the Spirit to the newly baptized by laying on hands, and confirmation continues this act (Catechism 1288). In the Latin church the bishop, successor of the apostles, is the ordinary minister of confirmation, which links the confirmed to the apostolic church (Catechism 1312–1313); a priest may confirm with the bishop's authority.

Chrismation is given by the priest right after baptism, anointing the newly baptized with the words "the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit." The holy chrism itself is consecrated by the bishops, so the apostolic laying on of hands reaches each believer through it.

Confirmation is given by a bishop with the laying on of hands, "after the example of thy holy Apostles" (Book of Common Prayer, 1662). But the Thirty-Nine Articles do not count it among the sacraments of the Gospel (Article 25).

Confirmation is a church custom of teaching and blessing, not a sacrament commanded by God (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 13). Any pastor may confirm. The Spirit is given through the word and baptism, not through a later rite.

Calvin held that the laying on of hands in Acts 8 gave the visible, miraculous gifts of the Spirit, which belonged to the apostles' time and have ceased; making it a sacrament insults baptism (Institutes 4.19.4–13). A profession of faith may follow instruction, but it adds nothing to baptism.

The Samaritans had believed and been baptized, and still received the Spirit later: an example of baptism in the Spirit as an experience after conversion, open to every believer through prayer, often with laying on of hands by any believer, not tied to an office (see the card at 19:2–6).

traditions.q: Philip and the eunuch "went down into the water" and "came up" (8:38–39). Must baptism be by immersion?
views: Yes. Baptism means immersion, the New Testament shows people going down into the water, and only immersion pictures burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:4). Baptism is "the immersion of a believer in water" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article VII).
Baptism is normally by three full immersions in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, even for infants. Pouring is accepted only in need.
Triple immersion is the most expressive form, but baptism may also be given by pouring water three times over the head, the usual Western practice (Catechism 1239).

"Dipping of the person into the water is not necessary; but baptism is rightly administered by pouring or sprinkling water upon the person" (Westminster Confession 28.3). Going "into" the water does not prove the person was put under.

Luther wished that those baptized were fully immersed, since baptism means drowning the old self and rising new (Sermon on Baptism, 1519). Yet Lutheran churches normally pour water, holding that the form is free when water and God's word are used; the tradition values immersion without requiring it.

Churches of Christ and related Restoration churches baptize only by immersion, following the New Testament examples, and teach that baptism is the point at which a believer's sins are forgiven (2:38; 22:16), as Alexander Campbell argued in The Christian System (1835).

title: The persecutor called
sum: Saul sets out for Damascus with the high priest's letters to arrest followers of the Way. Near the city a light from heaven throws him to the ground and a voice asks, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" It is Jesus. Blind, Saul is led into Damascus and waits three days without food. The Lord sends a frightened disciple, Ananias, to lay hands on him: this man is the vessel chosen to carry Jesus' name to Gentiles, kings and Israel, and he will suffer for it. Saul's sight returns, he is baptized, and at once he is in the synagogues proclaiming Jesus as the Son of God and the Messiah.

The hunter becomes the hunted. Plots in Damascus force him over the wall in a basket; in Jerusalem the disciples fear him until Barnabas vouches for him, and the Hellenists, Stephen's old opponents, try to kill him, so the believers send him home to Tarsus. The church across Judea, Galilee and Samaria has peace and grows. The chapter ends with Peter on tour: a paralyzed man, Aeneas, healed at Lydda, and a woman disciple, Tabitha, raised from death at Joppa, where Peter lodges with a tanner, one step from the house of a Gentile.
readings: For most of church history this is the classic conversion: a sinner, enemy of Christ, overwhelmed by grace and turned around in a moment. Augustine, Luther and Wesley read their own lives in its light, and "Damascus road" became a phrase for any sudden change of mind.

Krister Stendahl argued that Paul himself never speaks of a conversion from one religion to another but of a call, like Jeremiah's or Isaiah's (Galatians 1:15–16; Jeremiah 1:5; Isaiah 49:1–6). Saul does not stop worshiping Israel's God; he learns who Israel's Messiah is and is sent to the nations. Many now hold both: a call that turned his life upside down.

Paul tells parts of this story himself (Galatians 1:13–24; 1 Corinthians 15:8–10; 2 Corinthians 11:32–33; Philippians 3:4–11). The two accounts agree on the persecution, the appearance of Jesus, Damascus and the escape in a basket, and differ on the stay in Arabia, the timing of the Jerusalem visit and whom Saul met there. Readers weigh Paul's first-hand account and Luke's later narrative differently.

views.H: Damascus, a large city with many Jews, lay outside Judea; its control in the mid-30s (Roman, or the Nabatean king Aretas IV) is debated, and 2 Corinthians 11:32 shows Aretas' official involved in watching for Paul. Most date Saul's call between AD 31 and 36. Straight Street and Lydda, Joppa and the Sharon plain are real places on the map; Peter's route follows the old road from Jerusalem to the coast.
views.C: Luke tells Paul's call three times (9; 22; 26) with differences in detail: who heard the voice (9:7; 22:9), whether Ananias delivers the commission (9:15) or Jesus does on the road (26:16–18), the goads saying (26:14). Critical scholars see these as Luke's narrative variations or as traces of different sources; conservative scholars as complementary retellings for different audiences. Galatians 1 is usually given priority where it differs from Acts.
views.L: The chapter mirrors chapter 10: two visions that meet (Saul and Ananias; Cornelius and Peter), a reluctant messenger, and a crossing of boundaries. Saul's blindness and restored sight anticipate his task "to open their eyes" (26:18). Peter's healing of Aeneas and raising of Tabitha repeat Jesus' deeds (Luke 5:17–26; 8:49–56), linking the church's leaders to their Lord.
views.J: Saul was a Pharisee zealous for the Law (Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:5–6), and his campaign was an internal Jewish discipline of a sect he saw as dangerous. Jewish scholars such as Alan Segal read his experience as a Jewish visionary's encounter with God's glory and a real conversion between Jewish communities; Paula Fredriksen and others stress that he remained a Jew all his life. "The Jews" of 9:23 means the leaders in Damascus, not the Jewish people.
views.T: The church keeps the Conversion of Saint Paul as a feast (25 January in the West). The fathers saw in Ananias' laying on of hands and Saul's baptism a picture of Christian initiation, and in Peter's raising of Tabitha the power of prayer. Dorcas societies, women's groups sewing for the poor, took their name from 9:36–39.

deep.h: The three accounts of Saul's call
deep.b:
Acts 9 is the narrator's telling: light, voice, blindness, Ananias' vision, and the commission given to Ananias (9:15–16). Acts 22 is Paul's speech to a hostile Jewish crowd in Jerusalem: he stresses his zeal for the Law, describes Ananias as "a devout man according to the Law," and adds a later vision in the temple sending him to the Gentiles (22:17–21). Acts 26 is Paul's defense before King Agrippa: Ananias drops out, Jesus himself gives the commission on the road, quoting the prophets' language of being sent "to open their eyes" (26:16–18), and adds the proverb about kicking against the goads (26:14).

The differences fit the audiences: Jewish piety for a Jewish crowd, prophetic commission for a king who "believes the prophets" (26:27). Some see Luke's skill as a writer, others traces of different sources, and a few real contradictions (see the note at 9:7). The site translates the shared Greek words the same way in all three chapters, so readers can compare them.

Paul's own account (Galatians 1:13–24): after God revealed his Son to him, he did not consult anyone, went to Arabia, came back to Damascus, and after three years went to Jerusalem for fifteen days to visit Cephas, seeing only James besides; then he went to Syria and Cilicia, unknown by face to the churches of Judea. Acts compresses this and has Barnabas bring him to "the apostles" and Saul preach openly in Jerusalem. Harmonizers place Arabia inside the "considerable time" of 9:23 and take "the apostles" loosely. Critics conclude that Luke presents Paul as closer to Jerusalem than he was. Both agree that the basket escape (9:25; 2 Corinthians 11:33) is one of the clearest points of contact between Acts and the letters.

deep.title: Claude's theory: blinded so that he could open eyes
deep.b: In 26:18 Jesus sends Paul to the Gentiles "to open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light," words that echo the servant of Isaiah sent "to open blind eyes" (Isaiah 42:7, 16). I suggest Luke shaped chapter 9 so that Paul first lives through what he will preach: he sees the light, is plunged into three days of darkness, and has his eyes opened through another's hands. His blindness is then not only a punishment or a sign of shock but a rehearsal of his mission, and the phrase "something like scales" marks the moment the commission begins. Commentators have often linked Saul's blindness with the light-and-darkness language of 26:18 (for example Robert Tannehill); the reading of the blindness as a deliberate rehearsal of the commission is my own emphasis.

echoes: Genesis 22:11; Exodus 3:4; 1 Samuel 3:10; Isaiah 6:8; Isaiah 42:6–7; Isaiah 49:6; Jeremiah 1:5; Joshua 2:15; 1 Samuel 19:12; 1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:32–37; 1 Maccabees 15:21; Mark 5:35–43; Luke 5:17–26; Luke 8:49–56; 22:3–21; 26:9–23; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 1 Corinthians 15:8–10; 2 Corinthians 11:32–33; Galatians 1:13–24; Philippians 3:4–11

settings.what: The voice of Jesus on the Damascus road
settings.to: Saul, thrown to the ground, with his traveling companions hearing the voice but seeing no one
settings.when: as Saul nears Damascus with letters to arrest believers
settings.why: Jesus names Saul twice, as God called the patriarchs and prophets, and confronts him with what he is doing: persecuting Jesus himself in his people. He gives no explanation yet, only an order to go into the city and wait. The words were meant to stop Saul in his tracks and turn his zeal around.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, Paul was the hero of the second half of Acts; this scene showed that his authority came from the risen Lord himself, not from the Jerusalem leaders, and that God can turn even an enemy into a messenger.
views: Many, following Stendahl, read the words as a prophet's call (compare 26:16–18).
Others stress the turning from persecutor to believer and the baptism that follows.

settings.what: The Lord's commission given to Ananias
settings.by: the Lord Jesus, in a vision
settings.to: Ananias, a disciple in Damascus, who knew Saul's reputation
settings.when: during Saul's three days of blindness
settings.why: The Lord overrules Ananias' fear and reveals Saul's future: a chosen vessel to carry Jesus' name to Gentiles, kings and Israel, and to suffer for it. The words were meant to send a frightened believer to his enemy with open hands.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the speech is Acts' table of contents for Paul's career, and it told readers that Paul's suffering in the story to come was part of God's plan, not a sign of failure.

settings.what: Ananias' greeting and laying on of hands
settings.to: Saul, blind and fasting in Judas' house on Straight Street
settings.when: after Ananias' vision
settings.why: Ananias calls Saul "brother," names Jesus as the one who appeared to him, and lays hands on him for sight and the Spirit. The words welcome the enemy into the community before his baptism.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the scene showed that Paul was received and baptized by an ordinary Jewish believer in Damascus, and modeled the church's welcome of converts.

settings.what: Saul's preaching in the synagogues of Damascus
settings.to: the Jews of Damascus in their synagogues, many of whom had expected him to arrest the believers
settings.when: in the days right after his baptism
settings.why: Saul proclaims that Jesus is the Son of God and proves from the Scriptures that he is the Messiah. His hearers are astounded because he had come to silence that very message. His turnabout itself was part of the argument.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the scene set the pattern of Paul's mission in Acts: to the synagogue first, with proof from the Scriptures, and opposition that drives him on.

settings.what: Saul's preaching and debates in Jerusalem
settings.to: the Hellenists, Greek-speaking Jews of Jerusalem, the same group that had opposed Stephen (6:9)
settings.when: on his first visit to Jerusalem after his call
settings.why: Saul speaks boldly in Jesus' name and argues with the very people he had once sided with against Stephen. Their attempt to kill him shows that he has taken Stephen's place.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the scene closed the circle begun at Stephen's death (7:58; 8:1): the one who approved of Stephen's killing now faced the same danger for the same message.
views: Saul moved freely with the apostles and preached in Jerusalem.
Paul says he saw only Peter and James and was unknown by face to the churches of Judea (Galatians 1:18–22).

settings.what: Peter's word to Aeneas
settings.to: Aeneas, a man paralyzed for eight years, at Lydda
settings.when: on Peter's tour of the churches
settings.why: Peter heals in Jesus' name, not his own: "Jesus Christ is healing you." The command to get up and make his bed shows the man restored to ordinary life.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the healing linked Peter's work to Jesus' own healing of a paralyzed man (Luke 5:17–26) and showed the risen Lord still at work through his apostles.

settings.what: The Joppa disciples' plea to Peter
settings.by: two men sent by the disciples at Joppa
settings.to: Peter, at Lydda
settings.when: after Tabitha's death, while her body lies in an upstairs room
settings.why: "Do not hesitate; come on over to us" is an urgent request, though it does not ask for a miracle in so many words. The disciples send for the apostle because Tabitha mattered to the whole community, as the widows' grief shows (9:39), and perhaps because they had heard of Aeneas (9:35).
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's churches, late in the first century, the plea showed a small church turning to the apostles in grief, and God answering through them.

settings.what: Peter's prayer and command at Tabitha's body
settings.to: Tabitha, dead, in an upstairs room at Joppa, after the widows have been sent out
settings.when: after the disciples of Joppa sent for him from Lydda
settings.why: Peter kneels and prays first, then speaks: "Tabitha, get up." The scene repeats Jesus' raising of Jairus' daughter, which Peter had witnessed (Mark 5:37–41), and the prayers of Elijah and Elisha.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the story honored a woman disciple's service to the poor and showed Peter acting as Jesus did, just before God sends him to the Gentiles.

title: A Gentile house and a sheet from heaven
sum: At Caesarea, a Roman centurion named Cornelius, a Gentile who fears Israel's God, prays and gives to the poor, sees an angel at the afternoon hour of prayer: send to Joppa for Simon Peter. The next day, on a rooftop in Joppa, the hungry Peter falls into a trance and sees a sheet let down from heaven full of every kind of animal. A voice tells him to kill and eat; he refuses, since he has never eaten anything common and unclean; the voice answers, "What God has made clean, you must not call common." Three times. As he puzzles over it, Cornelius' men are at the gate, and the Spirit tells him to go with them without hesitating.

Peter enters a Gentile house, something his people did not do, and says God has shown him not to call any human being common or unclean. He tells the household the story of Jesus, from John's baptism to the cross and the resurrection, and promises forgiveness to everyone who believes. Before he finishes, the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear, and they speak in tongues, as the apostles had at Pentecost. Peter's Jewish companions are astounded, and Peter asks who could refuse them baptism. The longest story in Acts has reached its turning point: Gentiles belong to God's people without first becoming Jews.
readings: Peter later says the Spirit fell on Cornelius' household "the same way he fell on us in the beginning" (11:15). Luke tells the story three times (10; 11:1–18; 15:7–9) because it is the church's charter for the Gentile mission: God, not Peter, decided who belonged.

The story is as much about Peter as about Cornelius. The faithful Jew who had never eaten anything common is taught by a vision, by the Spirit, by events and finally by the Spirit's falling on Gentiles, and he changes his mind. Many readers see the hardest conversion in the chapter as the believer's, not the outsider's.
Read as a story about tables

Food and hospitality run through the chapter: Peter staying with a tanner, hungry at noon, a vision of animals, Gentile guests lodged in a Jewish house, a Jew entering a Gentile home, eating with the risen Jesus, and an invitation to stay. The question behind the vision is who may eat with whom, which became the burning issue at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14).

views.H: Caesarea Maritima was Herod's showpiece port and the Roman governor's capital, with a mostly Gentile population and a large Jewish minority. Centurions were career officers; God-fearers like Cornelius are attested by Josephus and by inscriptions such as the one at Aphrodisias. The date is uncertain: if Roman troops were withdrawn from Caesarea during Agrippa I's reign (AD 41–44), the story fits best before 41.
views.C: Martin Dibelius argued that Luke built the chapter from a simple local story of a God-fearer's conversion, adding the vision and the speech to make it the decisive precedent for the Gentile mission. Others think the vision originally concerned food, and that Luke applied it to people (10:28). Peter's speech, with its clipped outline of Jesus' life, is often taken as Luke's summary of early preaching (C. H. Dodd).
views.L: Luke uses paired visions, repetition (the angel's message is told four times: 10:3–6, 22, 30–32; 11:13–14) and delays to build suspense and to make God's guidance unmistakable. Peter's speech is a little Gospel. The repeated "stop" (8:36; 10:47; 11:17) ties the eunuch's baptism to this one.
views.J: No law of Moses forbade entering a Gentile's house; the barrier was custom and concern about food and idols, as Jubilees and the Mishnah show. Peter's companions and the Jerusalem believers (11:2–3) are troubled, not because they hate Gentiles but because faithfulness to the covenant was at stake. Jewish readers note that the decision here, as later at the council (15), set the pattern for a church in which Gentiles did not keep the Torah's distinctive laws.
views.T: The fathers saw here the calling of the nations, foretold by the prophets (Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts). The Spirit's coming before baptism became a key text in debates over Spirit and sacrament; 10:47–48 is cited both for the necessity of baptism and for the freedom of the Spirit. Peter's refusal of Cornelius' bowing is cited in debates over the veneration of saints.

deep.h: Why the story is told three times
deep.b:
Acts tells Cornelius' conversion in full here, again in Peter's report to Jerusalem (11:1–18), and in summary at the council (15:7–11). Only Paul's call gets the same treatment. Repetition was an ancient storyteller's way of saying "this matters." Each telling shifts the emphasis: chapter 10 follows events as they happened; chapter 11 defends Peter's eating with Gentiles; chapter 15 draws the rule: God "made no distinction" and cleansed their hearts by faith, so Gentile believers need not be circumcised.

The Plain uses the same English for the same Greek across the three tellings, above all the fixed words "Get up, Peter; kill and eat" and "What God has made clean, you must not call common," so readers can see what each retelling keeps and changes.

The vision speaks of animals; Peter applies it to people (10:28); and the Jerusalem believers complain about table fellowship (11:3). How do the three connect? In Leviticus the separation of clean and unclean animals was tied to Israel's separation from the nations: "I have set you apart from the peoples to be mine" (Leviticus 20:26). If God now declares the animals clean, the wall that the food laws symbolized and protected is down. Most Christian readers have taken the vision to end the food laws for all believers; others, among them Seventh-day Adventists and many Messianic Jews, hold that it concerns people only. The notes at 10:14–15 and 10:28 give the readings.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Jonah's journey reversed
deep.b: Peter is in Joppa, the port where Jonah boarded a ship to flee from God's call to preach to the Gentile city of Nineveh (Jonah 1:3). Jesus had called Peter "Simon Bar-Jonah," son of Jonah (Matthew 16:17). Now another son of Jonah, in the same port, is called to a Gentile household, objects ("Not at all, Lord!"), and then goes. I suggest Luke, who mentions Joppa by name ten times in chapters 9–11, means readers who know their Bible to feel the echo: the disciple does what the prophet refused, and the story ends not with a sulking prophet but with Gentiles praising God. The Jonah-Joppa link has been noticed by several commentators; Luke never names Jonah here, and the connection to Peter's patronymic is my own suggestion and may be accidental.

echoes: Genesis 1:24–25; Genesis 6:20; Leviticus 2:2; Leviticus 11; Leviticus 20:24–26; Deuteronomy 10:17; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Psalm 107:20; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 56:7; Isaiah 61:1; Ezekiel 1:1; Ezekiel 4:14; Daniel 9:21; Jonah 1:3; Tobit 12:12; Luke 3:21–22; Luke 4:18; Luke 7:1–10; Luke 24:36–49; 2:1–4; 11:1–18; 15:7–11; Galatians 2:11–14; Romans 10:12; Romans 14:14

settings.what: The angel's message to Cornelius
settings.to: Cornelius, a Gentile centurion at Caesarea who feared God
settings.when: at the ninth hour, the afternoon time of prayer
settings.why: The angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and alms have reached God like an offering and that he must send for Peter. The message honors the piety of a Gentile who could not offer at the temple, and sets in motion the meeting that will bring him the gospel (11:14).
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, perhaps many of them Gentiles who had once been God-fearers (who Luke's readers were is debated: see the views on the book's opening page), the scene told them that God had seen people like them before the church came to them.

settings.what: The voice in Peter's vision
settings.to: Peter, in a trance on the roof of Simon the tanner's house at Joppa
settings.when: at noon, while he waited, hungry, for a meal
settings.why: The voice orders Peter to kill and eat from a sheet full of clean and unclean animals, and when he refuses, declares that what God has made clean he must not call common. The words were meant to break a lifelong boundary, first about food and, as Peter grasps, about people (10:28).
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the vision answered the question that divided many churches: whether Jewish and Gentile believers could share one table.
views: Most readers take the words to end the food laws and the separation they stood for.
Some hold that Peter's own application (10:28) limits the vision to people, and that the food laws were not abolished.

settings.what: The Spirit's order to Peter
settings.to: Peter, still puzzling over the vision
settings.when: as Cornelius' messengers stand at the gate
settings.why: The Spirit tells Peter to go with the men without hesitating, "for I am the one who sent them." The words link the vision to the visitors and take away Peter's excuse.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the Spirit's direct command meant that the Gentile mission was not Peter's idea or Paul's, but God's.

settings.what: Peter and Cornelius' messengers
settings.to: Cornelius' two servants and soldier at the gate, and then Peter
settings.when: as they reach Simon the tanner's house in Joppa
settings.why: Peter's question, "What has brought you here?", lets the messengers state their errand. They speak for their master in terms a Jew would want to hear: Cornelius is righteous, fears God, is well spoken of by "the whole Jewish nation," and was told by a holy angel to listen to Peter. Peter answers by taking Gentiles in as his guests, a first step over the line he will name in 10:28.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's churches, late in the first century, the messengers' words set out why a Gentile like Cornelius could be welcomed, and Peter's hospitality showed the welcome beginning even before he left Joppa.

settings.what: Peter's words to Cornelius at the door and inside his house
settings.to: Cornelius, his relatives and close friends, all Gentiles, with six Jewish believers from Joppa
settings.when: on arriving in Caesarea
settings.why: At the door Peter refuses Cornelius' bow: "I am a human being myself" (10:26). Inside he names the custom he is breaking and the reason: God has shown him that no person is to be called common or unclean. The words reassure the Gentiles that he comes willingly and explain to his Jewish companions why he has crossed the line.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the scene gave them the founding precedent for mixed Jewish and Gentile churches.

settings.what: Cornelius' account of his vision
settings.to: Peter and the Jewish believers with him
settings.when: after Peter asks why he was sent for
settings.why: Cornelius retells the angel's visit and declares that his household is gathered "before God" to hear what the Lord has commanded Peter to say. His words show an ideal hearer: ready, humble and expectant.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, Cornelius was a model of how Gentiles should receive the message: as hearers of God's word, not of a man's.

settings.what: Peter's sermon in Cornelius' house
settings.to: a Gentile household: Cornelius, his relatives and close friends, people who knew something of Jesus' story from living in Judea
settings.when: in Caesarea, a few days after Peter's vision
settings.why: Peter begins with what he has just learned, that God accepts people of every nation, then tells the story of Jesus from John's baptism to the cross and resurrection, naming the apostles as witnesses and Jesus as Lord of all and judge of all. He ends with the offer of forgiveness to everyone who believes. Speaking to Gentiles, he blames "they" for Jesus' death, not his hearers, and he needs to explain Jesus' anointing and Israel's prophets. The speech was meant to bring the household to faith; the Spirit's coming interrupted it.
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the sermon gave a short, complete Gospel in the form the church preached to Gentiles, and showed Peter, the leader of the Twelve, as the first to welcome the nations.
views: Many, following C. H. Dodd, think the speech preserves the outline of early apostolic preaching, close to Mark's Gospel.
Others, following Martin Dibelius, see it as Luke's own summary written for this scene, as ancient historians composed speeches.

settings.what: Peter's question about baptism
settings.to: his Jewish companions from Joppa, in Cornelius' house
settings.when: after the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles
settings.why: Peter asks a question no one can answer: who could refuse water to people who have received the Spirit as the apostles did? The question was meant to bind his Jewish companions to what God had done, so that they would stand with him in Jerusalem (11:12).
settings.readers: For Theophilus and Luke's mostly Gentile churches, late in the first century, the words became the church's answer to anyone who wanted to set extra conditions on Gentile believers.

traditions.q: Cornelius bowed down at Peter's feet, and Peter lifted him up: "I am a human being myself" (10:25–26). Is it right to bow before or venerate holy people?
views: Worship (latria) belongs to God alone, but honor (dulia) may rightly be given to the saints as friends of God; Peter refused an act that could be mistaken for worship of a man. The Church distinguishes the honor paid to images and saints from adoration of God (Catechism 2132; compare 971).

The Second Council of Nicaea (787) distinguished the veneration (proskynēsis, bowing) given to icons and saints from the worship (latreia) due to God alone. Bowing before a holy person or icon honors God's work in them.
The saints may be remembered and honored as examples of faith and of God's grace, but Scripture does not teach calling on them or giving them religious honor (Augsburg Confession, article 21).

Religious worship is to be given to God alone, "and to him alone; not to angels, saints, or any other creature" (Westminster Confession 21.2). Peter's words and the angel's in Revelation 19:10 forbid bowing in religious honor to any creature.

Religious worship belongs to God alone, and there is no mediator but Christ (Second London Baptist Confession 22.2; Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article II). Peter's answer, "I am a human being myself," shows that church leaders, however honored, must refuse any reverence that belongs to God.
